A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenRubrics research, with matching authors, framework, and experiments. All 30 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Rubric-RM evaluations, policy-training results, inference timings, and qualitative case studies in Sections 5.2–5.6.

after.justification: v2 retains original reward-model and policy experiments, revises several results, and adds original Rubric-RM policy results on WildBench in Table 4.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 adds listwise rubric curation: ordered responses induce pairwise comparisons, and rubrics survive when at least 50% agree with preference labels. Appendix B.4 supplies the corresponding generation prompt and revises general-domain judging to require explicit gatekeeper reasoning and an aggregation summary. These extend the existing CRG/filtering procedure while retaining the two-stage architecture and SFT objectives.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 and Figure 2 replace the Tulu 2.5 and HelpSteer3 training-source components with Magpie's synthetic general-domain instructions. v2 also adds WildBench policy evaluation across creative, planning, mathematics, information-seeking, and coding tasks. Together these substantially revise training coverage and broaden evaluation. Tulu3-IF/Synthetic-IF is a renamed retained source, rather than an independently added task.

E2.justification: The added WildBench comparison includes new comparators DRIFT, GPT-4-turbo, and GPT-4o-mini, with their results attributed to prior work. Existing comparator membership in Tables 1–3 and the HealthBench comparison is retained. Table 4 names DRIFT; the accompanying prose inconsistently calls it DRN.

E3.justification: WildBench introduces task-specific scores and a task-macro WB score, with RLCF and RLMT evaluated using official checkpoints. Existing training and sampling parameter entries in Tables 7–8 are identical across versions, and retained benchmark metrics and model sizes remain unchanged. The added evaluation does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Both case studies remain, but their displayed rubrics and judging rationales change. In particular, the FollowBench case moves from v1 Table 6 to v2 Table 9 and changes its gatekeeper from quotation evidence to an explicit stance on financial viability. Appendix A also adds a distribution analysis counted by preference pairs. No new component-ablation or robustness suite appears.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, confidence intervals, standard errors, or significance tests. The five independently sampled judge trajectories used for voting@5 are retained; this remains an inference ensemble rather than new uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces results for the proposed models and naive Qwen pipeline: Rubric-RM-8B averages 68.5 in v1 and 70.1 in v2, while voting@5 changes from 71.2 to 73.0. Policy results also change: IFBench falls from 33.7 to 30.3, and the Arena-Hard/AlpacaEval average changes from 50.6 to 48.6. WildBench adds a 53.6 macro score. HealthBench scores and efficiency timings remain unchanged. Changed data and prompt specifications prevent treating these as controlled cross-version gains or losses.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 corrects the inference mapping from g_theta(x, y_A, y_B) to g_theta(x), aligning it with the prompt-only SFT objective and generation template already present in v1. This is a limited correction to the formal conditioning specification. The remaining reward definitions and training losses are equivalent, and neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The dataset, CRG, and rubric-based alignment contributions remain. The introduction and conclusion strengthen the reported reward-model improvement from 6.8% to 8.4%, while removing the earlier quantified policy-gain summaries of 2.9% and 1.1%–6.5%. The abstract still states 6.8%, creating an internal inconsistency.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning inherited model/data biases, subjective and culturally nuanced criteria, the scope of pairwise reward evaluation, and untested online RLHF and long-horizon learning. v1 primarily offered future-work directions without these explicit qualifications. The central interpretations of rubric-guided judging and domain-specific training remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds the listwise template and distinguishes general-domain and medical judging prompts; Appendix A newly reports 85.6k preference pairs, separately from instruction counts. Conversely, v1's description of sampling four responses per HealthBench question for DPO is omitted. Training/sampling hyperparameters and model/data access links are retained.

R1.justification: Magpie and DRIFT are newly cited, while citations associated with removed training sources, including Tulu 2.5 and HelpSteer3, disappear alongside several other references. The related-work argument positioning scalable rubric synthesis against frontier-model prompting and iterative rubric refinement remains substantially unchanged. Publication-metadata updates do not introduce additional works.

P1.justification: The method and experimental narratives undergo extensive condensation and rewriting, especially Sections 4.3 and 5.2–5.6. Biomedical subsections are merged, decoding details and the second case study move to the appendix, and the former appendix is reorganized into rubric statistics and implementation details. A separate Limitations section is added.

P2.justification: v2 revises the source-distribution chart and t-SNE display, adds WildBench Table 4 and preference-pair Figure 6, substantially reformats the case-study tables, and relocates the FollowBench case. Table captions move below tables, while prompt boxes are resized and reflowed extensively. These constitute broad display and layout changes beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly strengthens validation and transparency through the WildBench evaluation, clearer prompt-only inference, expanded curation templates, and explicit applicability limitations. These benefits are tempered by the stale 6.8% abstract claim versus 8.4% in the introduction/conclusion and the loss of HealthBench response-sampling detail. The higher reward-model averages do not independently establish better quality because data and prompt specifications also change.
